# How to Use Picsart's AI Creative Tools: 4 Beginner Projects You Can Finish Today

> **In short:** Picsart's tutorials walk you through four projects: turning one product photo into a 3D model, animating a still photo with a dance clip, designing a YouTube banner that fits every screen, and starting a cartoon YouTube channel with an option to monetize through Picsart Earn, which Picsart describes as its program for creators.

You have a phone full of photos and a folder of half-started ideas. Maybe you sell something online and want better visuals. Maybe you want a YouTube channel but hate being on camera. Maybe you just want to see what AI can actually do today. Picsart, a popular photo and video editor, publishes step-by-step tutorials that walk ordinary users through four concrete AI projects. Let's follow them, one at a time.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- The Picsart app on your phone, or the desktop version
- A free Picsart account (some templates may require a paid plan — check Picsart's pricing page for current tiers)
- A folder with 3–5 well-lit photos of your product, your face, or your logo
- About 15–30 minutes for your first project

Picsart's tutorials are organized inside what the source describes as the **Flow workspace** — a visual area where you connect small AI tasks together, like LEGO blocks that each do one job. Open Picsart, look for the section the source calls the Flow workspace, and you'll find the project tutorials listed there.

## Step 1 — Turn one product photo into a 3D model

This is the easiest "wow" project for first-timers.

1. Open the Flow workspace and find the **3D Product Visualization** tutorial.
2. Pick one clear, well-lit photo of your product — a sneaker, a candle, a mug, anything with visible edges.
3. Drop the photo into the project's starting step. The AI takes a moment to study your object.
4. The output is a **GLB model** — a standard 3D file format you can rotate, view from any angle, and share online. No 3D software, no hand-drawn shapes.
5. Save the file when you're happy with the result.

💬 Example prompt if the template asks for one: *"white ceramic mug with handle facing left, on a wooden table"*

You'll know it worked when you can spin the model around with your finger or mouse and see the back, top, and sides of your product.

## Step 2 — Animate a still photo with a dance clip

This one feels like a magic trick the first time you see it.

1. In the Flow workspace, open the animation or photo-to-video tutorial.
2. Choose your starting photo: a clear portrait where the person's full body or upper body is visible.
3. Pick a method. Picsart's tutorial describes two:
   - **Reference dance:** upload a short video of someone dancing. The AI transfers those moves to the person in your photo.
   - **Prompt from scratch:** type what you want, and the AI generates the dance.
4. Type your dance description or upload your reference video.
5. Generate, preview, and save the result.

💬 Example prompt: *"hip-hop routine"* or *"slow-motion spin"* — phrases Picsart's own tutorial lists as starting points.

You'll know it worked when the still photo moves like a short video clip and the person's face stays recognizably them throughout the dance.

## Step 3 — Design a YouTube banner that fits every screen

A **YouTube banner** is the wide image at the top of a channel. The tricky part: YouTube crops it differently on phones, TVs, and desktop, so the important parts (your name, logo) need to sit in the center **safe area** — the middle zone that doesn't get cut off on any device.

1. Open the Flow workspace and find the YouTube banner tutorial.
2. Describe your channel in a **prompt** — the instruction you type to the AI, like telling an artist what to paint.
3. Optionally upload a portrait or logo for the AI to follow.
4. Generate the art at **16:9 aspect ratio** (the shape of a widescreen image) and **2560 × 1440 pixels** — the size YouTube recommends, per Picsart's tutorial.
5. Tweak any detail, download the file, and upload it inside **YouTube Studio** — the dashboard at studio.youtube.com where creators manage their channels.

💬 Example prompt: *"clean gradient banner with my channel name 'Tasty Tuesdays' in bold white text, food illustrations around the edges"*

You'll know it worked when your name and logo are clearly visible on phone, desktop, and TV previews without being cut off.

## Step 4 — Build a cartoon YouTube channel, from cast to payout

If you've ever wanted to run a channel but felt camera-shy, this is the full loop Picsart's tutorial outlines.

1. In the Flow workspace, open the cartoon video tutorial.
2. Use the AI tools to create your cartoon characters — what Picsart calls the "cast".
3. Animate short videos using the same tools you tried in Step 2.
4. Export at YouTube's recommended **specs** — the technical settings YouTube prefers (resolution, file format) so your video uploads cleanly and plays smoothly.
5. When ready, look into **Picsart Earn** — a program for creators to earn from their work, according to Picsart — to see whether you qualify.

💬 Example prompt for a character: *"friendly cartoon chef with a red bandana, big eyes, simple round shapes"*

You'll know it worked when you've posted at least one cartoon video to YouTube and explored Picsart Earn's signup flow to see whether you qualify.

## Step 5 — Chain two projects in one Flow (the fun part)

Now that you've seen how each piece works, you can connect them.

1. Open a new project in the Flow workspace.
2. Start with one of the steps from above — for example, generate a cartoon character using the prompts from Step 4.
3. Connect that character into the animation step from Step 2.
4. Add your finished animation into a banner design from Step 3 as a background element.
5. Save the full chain as one project.

💬 Example flow: *"cartoon chef"* → *"waving and dancing"* → *"used as the right-side accent of a YouTube banner"*

You'll know it worked when you see your character move inside a banner you made — all without leaving the Flow workspace.

## Common mistakes

- **Picking a busy photo for the 3D step.** A cluttered background makes the AI guess the wrong edges. Use a clean shot against a plain wall or table.
- **Writing a vague dance prompt.** "Dance" alone gives random results. "Hip-hop routine" or "slow-motion spin" — the phrases Picsart's tutorial actually uses — give you something recognizable.
- **Forgetting the YouTube safe area.** A banner that looks great on desktop may cut off your name on phones. Always preview at phone, desktop, and TV sizes before publishing.
- **Skipping the paid-tier check.** Some Flow templates may require a plan beyond the free tier. Check Picsart's pricing page before starting a longer project, so you don't lose work halfway through.

## What this means for you

- **If you're selling something online (small business, side hustle, Etsy):** the 3D product trick alone could replace a stack of extra photos. One good product shot becomes a full 360° view in minutes.
- **If you post on social media but hate being on camera:** the cartoon channel path and the dancing-photo trick both let you create content without showing your face.
- **If you're starting a YouTube channel this week:** make the banner first. It takes ten minutes and instantly makes the channel look real.
- **If you already use Picsart:** try chaining two of these in the Flow workspace — for example, generate a cartoon character, then animate it dancing, then drop the still into your new banner. According to Picsart, the tools are designed to work together, so combining them is the natural next step.

## Wrap-up

You don't need a design degree or expensive software to make professional-looking visuals anymore. Start with the smallest project that excites you — maybe the dancing photo, since it takes under five minutes — and let the momentum carry you to the next one. Open Picsart, pick a tutorial, and follow it step by step. The best way to feel comfortable with these tools is to make one thing today.
